title: Spectral Signatures of Memorization Basins in Diffusion Trajectories

paper.title: Spectral Signatures of Memorization Basins in Diffusion Trajectories
paper.abstract:
Abstract Diffusion models are known to reproduce individual examples from their training data as a form of memorization with implications for generalization, privacy, and downstream use.
Recent work demonstrated that memorized training samples reside inside contiguous regions of the data/latent space known as basins of memorization – once a denoising trajectory enters a basin, under finite perturbations it irreversibly reproduces a memorized example.
Prior empirical work on such basins in trained models has primarily focused on classifier-free guidance based detection and mitigation strategies in text-to-image models, leaving basin entry in trained diffusion trajectories and the formation of such basins largely uncharacterized.
In this paper, we present a geometric characterization of memorization basins for conditional, unconditional, and rectified-flow-based diffusion models.
We observe a characteristic signature in the local spectrum of the function geometry that distinguishes basin entry: the emergence of a dominant singular mode followed by a sharp spectral recovery.
This signature appears at two timescales: along denoising trajectories during inference and over the course of training, with a markedly stronger presence along memorized trajectories.
We further investigate whether these geometric signatures can be used to intervene on memorization. During training, we suppress memorization by acting on the dominant mode. At inference, we develop methods to identify trajectories entering memorization basins and steer them away. We find that these interventions remain effective even with low-dimensional approximations of the underlying geometry, and demonstrate that geometry-informed steering extends to large-scale text-to-image diffusion models. Together, our results corroborate that local spectral geometry provides a common basis for characterizing memorization and for suppressing, detecting, and steering away from it across training and generation.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Generative models are increasingly deployed as components of larger computational systems, where their outputs inform subsequent predictions, optimization, or decisions. Diffusion models exemplify this shift as they are deployed to generate molecular and protein structures ( Wu et al., 2024 ) , candidate solutions for combinatorial optimization ( Sun and Yang, 2023 ) , and actions and trajectories for planning and control ( Chi et al., 2025 ) . As diffusion models take on this broader role, it is important to understand how much information from their training data is retained in their generated samples. Diffusion models can closely reproduce individual training examples ( Carlini et al., 2023 ) , raising concerns around privacy, copyright, and generalization. However, memorization is not inherently undesirable. More broadly in deep learning, retaining information about individual or atypical training examples can contribute positively to generalization ( Feldman and Zhang, 2020 ) . In diffusion models, memorization is also highly selective. These models reproduce only a subset of their training examples, with susceptibility to memorization depending on properties of both the data and the learned distribution ( Carlini et al., 2023 ; Bonnaire et al., 2026 ) . More generally, these empirical observations regarding memorization and memory in deep learning have been connected to model geometry. Previous work has shown that retained training information can be reflected in local model geometry ( Nickl et al., 2023 ) and captured through compact spectral representations ( Jung et al., 2026 ) . In generative models, the manifold memorization hypothesis further associates memorized samples with locally constrained regions of the learned distribution ( Ross et al., 2025 ) . In this work, we posit that the constrained local geometry associated with memorization have a distinct temporal signature as trajectories evolve during denoising. We further investigate whether this geometry can be used to identify and intervene on memorized trajectories. More specifically, we ask: when does a denoising trajectory become committed to a memorized outcome, what spectral signature emerges, and can it guide intervention? We adopt the framework of memorization basins , defining them as regions from which a trajectory cannot escape a memorized outcome under bounded perturbations. Around basin entry, we empirically observe a distinct signature in the local Jacobian spectrum, accompanied by changes in perturbation sensitivity and generative dynamics. A related spectral pattern also emerges during training. At intermediate denoising steps, the input-output Jacobians develop a dominant singular mode, whereas low-noise spectra exhibit stronger rank recovery. We further investigate whether these geometric properties can be used to suppress memorization during training and to detect or redirect memorized trajectories during generation. To this end, we propose GeoReg-DM, which regularizes local Jacobian geometry to suppress memorization during training. For inference, we introduce Jacobian Effective Rank (JER), which uses the endpoint of the spectral signature to detect memorized generations, and GeoSteer-DM, which exploits dominant singular directions to redirect memorized trajectories. Across diffusion and rectified-flow models, our results establish local spectral geometry as a unifying perspective on how memorization emerges and can be controlled across training and generation.

sections.heading: Memorization and geometry in generative models.
sections.text: Memorization is a longstanding phenomenon in overparameterized neural networks, which can retain individual or atypical training examples while still generalizing ( Feldman and Zhang, 2020 ) . In generative models, memorization becomes directly observable through training-example reproduction ( Carlini et al., 2023 ; Somepalli et al., 2023a ) , with subsequent work studying how it develops during diffusion training and how retained examples are represented within the model ( Bonnaire et al., 2026 ; Hintersdorf et al., 2024 ; Kowalczuk et al., 2025 ) . Local geometry provides a complementary perspective on generative distributions ( Meng et al., 2021 ) , including intrinsic dimensionality, manifold structure, and spectral regimes across diffusion time ( Stanczuk et al., 2024 ; Humayun et al., 2025 ; Ventura et al., 2025 ) . Memorization has specifically been associated with locally constrained or sharp regions of the learned distribution ( Ross et al., 2025 ; Jeon et al., 2024 ) , while related analyses study denoiser-Jacobian eigenstructure ( Kadkhodaie et al., 2024 ) , variance-dependent loss of tangent dimensions ( Achilli et al., 2024 ) , and log-probability anisotropy ( Asthana and Belagiannis, 2026 ) . We build on these analyses by resolving spectral geometry along individual trajectories and across training, and by using its singular directions for intervention.

sections.heading: Memorization mitigation and geometric control.
sections.text: Existing mitigation methods intervene during training through the data or optimization procedure ( Dutt et al., 2025 ; Shah et al., 2025 ) , or during generation through conditioning, attention, model predictions, initial noise, and internal model components ( Somepalli et al., 2023a ; Ren et al., 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ; Wen et al., 2024 ; Han et al., 2026 ) . Separately, geometric editing methods use Jacobian singular directions and learned subspaces to control generation ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Gaintseva et al., 2026b ; Gaintseva et al., 2026a ) . Our approach connects these perspectives by using memorization-associated local spectral geometry as an intervention target during training and as a signal for detection and control during generation.

sections.heading: Spectral collapse and recovery of denoising trajectories.
sections.text: We adopt the CelebA setting of Bonnaire et al. (2026) , training a U-Net diffusion model on 4,096 images and generating samples with DDIM. We classify a generation as memorized using the nearest-neighbor distance-ratio criterion of Yoon et al. (2023) . Along all denoising trajectories, the local Jacobian spectrum undergoes a phase transition, visible as a sharp rise in the relative spectral gap Δ 12 \Delta_{12} (Figure 1 a). In terms of stable rank, this transition appears as a spectral collapse followed by recovery (Appendix F.2 ). The dynamic is driven largely by the top singular value. During collapse, σ 1 \sigma_{1} overshoots the remaining singular values and concentrates the spectrum around a single dominant mode. During recovery, the remaining singular values catch up and the spectrum relaxes toward a more isotropic structure as generation approaches low noise. Memorized trajectories undergo a stronger version of this cycle, with a sharper overshoot of σ 1 \sigma_{1} followed by a more pronounced recovery. As a result, Δ 12 \Delta_{12} separates memorized from non-memorized trajectories at inference time (Figure 1 a). Because individual trajectories undergo collapse–recovery at different timesteps, we define t ∗ t^{*} as the state preceding the steepest increase in Δ 12 \Delta_{12} and align trajectories by τ = t − t ∗ \tau=t-t^{*} . After t ∗ t^{*} , memorized trajectories become substantially less sensitive to finite perturbations, and their predicted clean samples rapidly approach the final output (Figure 1 b–c). Over the same region, bounded adversarial perturbations progressively lose their ability to redirect trajectories away from memorized outcomes (Appendix F.1 ). Together, these results suggest that the spectral transition at t ∗ t^{*} is an observable marker of declining escapeability, i.e., of the region where trajectories enter the memorization basin.

sections.heading: Connecting dynamical collapse to local memorization geometry.
sections.text: This collapse–recovery dynamic bridges trajectory-level views of memorization ( Biroli et al., 2024 ; Achilli et al., 2024 ) with local geometric accounts ( Ross et al., 2025 ; Stanczuk et al., 2024 ) . While the geometry near a memorized endpoint approaches an isotropic I / b t I/b_{t} structure (Appendix A.5 ), trajectories reach this regime by first passing through a phase of strong spectral concentration around basin entry. This intermediate regime isolates a dominant singular direction near t ∗ t^{*} , providing the geometric direction that GeoSteer-DM later exploits to redirect memorized trajectories. sections.heading: Spectral concentration emerges during training.
sections.text: Furthermore, the geometric organization observed during denoising develops progressively during training (Figure 2 ). As training advances and population-level memorization increases, the local Jacobian becomes increasingly concentrated around a dominant mode at intermediate noise levels, reflected by a pronounced rise in the relative spectral gap Δ 12 \Delta_{12} around t ∈ [ 200,400 ] t\in[200,400] that grows with memorization rate (Figure 2 a). At lower noise levels ( t ≤ 200 t\leq 200 ), the spectral gap closes and the local entropy rank ν ⁡ ( J t ) \nu(J_{t}) recovers toward a less concentrated spectrum at later checkpoints (Figure 2 b). These observations provide a training-time regularization target, directly motivating our approach GeoReg-DM .

sections.heading: 4 CONTROLLING MEMORIZATION THROUGH SPECTRAL GEOMETRY
sections.text: Our geometric analysis highlights two key points of intervention: regularizing the dominant intermediate-noise mode during training, and using local singular directions to detect and steer trajectories at inference time. We translate these insights into three complementary mechanisms: GeoReg-DM for training, JER for detection, and GeoSteer-DM for inference-time steering.

sections.heading: 5 EXPERIMENTS
sections.text: We evaluate our framework in two complementary settings. We first train unconditional diffusion and rectified-flow models on a controlled CelebA subset, where memorization is measured by the nearest-neighbor gap ratio to the training set. We then test JER and GeoSteer-DM on Stable Diffusion v1.4, measuring memorization by SSCD similarity to known training references, and compare against existing inference-time baselines 1 1 1 Code will be released upon acceptance. . Complete experimental details are found in Appendix E .

sections.heading: 5.1 Suppression, Detection, and Steering in unconditional diffusion
sections.text: In the unconditional diffusion setting, we use our geometric framework to address three core questions: whether GeoReg-DM suppresses memorization while preserving coverage, whether JER detects memorized trajectories efficiently, and whether GeoSteer-DM redirects them.

sections.heading: Can GeoReg-DM suppress memorization without sacrificing distribution coverage?
sections.text: GeoReg-DM regularizes the local Jacobian geometry during training to suppress emerging memorization. We first evaluate it on three synthetic populations (Gaussian, Gaussian mixture, and 8D Swiss roll), where access to the true data distribution allows us to distinguish training-set copying from population coverage. Across all three settings, GeoReg-DM achieves the strongest reduction in copying while consistently preserving or improving recall (Table 1 ). This effect extends directly to image generation on CelebA32, where GeoReg-DM substantially reduces memorization and outperforms other approaches on both measures (Table 1 ). This decrease in memorization comes with only a modest increase in FID, which is expected in this setting: removing exact training-set reproductions can itself increase FID even when perceptual quality and sample diversity are preserved. We investigate this effect further, together with representative generations and additional perceptual-quality analyses, in Fig. 10 and Appendix F.3 . Together with the synthetic results, these findings show that GeoReg-DM suppresses memorization without simply contracting the learned distribution, and that this behavior transfers from controlled populations to image generation. To further highlight the impact of our regularization approach, we analyze the spectral geometry of the Jacobian after GeoReg regularization. We observe that the regularization affects the entire spectrum. Specifically, GeoReg significantly slows down concentration in the top singular value, as evidenced by Figure 12 . sections.heading: Local Jacobian geometry enables efficient post-hoc detection.
sections.text: As a baseline, we use temporal recovery, which follows directly from our spectral analysis and scores how strongly the spectrum recovers after its collapse along a trajectory. However, it requires full Jacobian spectra at multiple points along the trajectory, which makes it expensive. Comparing it with local terminal geometry on held-out CelebA trajectories shows that JER captures a strong memorization signal at substantially lower computational cost (Table 2 ). For DDIM, JER achieves the strongest overall detection, outperforming both local baselines and full temporal recovery. For rectified flow, temporal recovery achieves the best detection accuracy, while our faster approach JER still outperforms all other local geometric detectors. The main distinction between JER and temporal recovery lies in the richer temporal information available to the latter. These results point to differences in how memorization is geometrically encoded across sampling methods. We also note that the spectral recovery baseline is intended only to validate our geometric observations, not as a practical method, since computing the geometry over the full trajectory is very slow in practice. sections.heading: Local geometry enables actionable, low-rank trajectory steering.
sections.text: Using the full Jacobian spectrum, GeoSteer-DM substantially suppresses memorization across training checkpoints for both DDIM and rectified flow (Figure 3 ), reducing late-stage memorization from 51.6 % 51.6\% to 7.6 % 7.6\% and from 60.2 % 60.2\% to 8.0 % 8.0\% , respectively. Importantly, effective intervention does not require the full Jacobian. Here we observe that low-rank sketches with k ∈ { 8 , … , 64 } k\in\{8,\ldots,64\} retain sufficient directional information to substantially reduce memorization, and performance improves as geometric resolution increases. At k = 64 k=64 , aggregate memorization falls to 10.0 % 10.0\% for DDIM and 14.0 % 14.0\% for rectified flow. These results further corroborate that the spectral signature observed in our analysis is actionable for intervention, and that useful steering signals can be recovered without full Jacobian construction—a point we will highlight more extensively in the text-to-image diffusion experiments in the next section. Full-Jacobian steering gives the strongest suppression. Low-dimensional Jacobian sketches retain much of this effect, with suppression generally strengthening as k k increases.

sections.heading: 5.2 Scaling Geometric Steering to Text-to-Image Diffusion
sections.text: The controlled experiments establish that memorization geometry is both detectable and actionable, and that effective intervention directions can be recovered under low-rank approximations. We now test whether these properties scale to Stable Diffusion v1.4, where text conditioning and high dimensionality make full Jacobian construction infeasible. Using matrix-free estimates of the guidance-residual Jacobian (Appendix C.2 ), we evaluate GeoSteer-DM across 500 prompts with known memorized references (2,000 generations per setup).

sections.heading: Geometric steering scales to text-to-image diffusion.
sections.text: Using matrix-free estimates of local guidance geometry, GeoSteer-DM substantially reduces training-reference similarity and the fraction of generations exceeding the SSCD copying threshold, while generation quality and a modest reduction in prompt alignment (Figure 4 ; full metrics in Appendix F.12 ). This demonstrates that local geometric steering scales to large-scale text-conditioned models. Representative samples in Figure 15 illustrate this and show that steering suppresses memorization while preserving core prompt semantics.

sections.heading: GeoSteer-DM complements existing mitigation strategies.
sections.text: Unlike existing methods that intervene via text conditioning, attention, model predictions, or initial noise, GeoSteer-DM acts directly on local Jacobian geometry. As shown in Figure 4 , adding GeoSteer-DM consistently shifts each baseline toward lower reference similarity with minimal impact on CLIP score or FID. Furthermore, these shifts are smaller on non-memorized control prompts (Appendix F.12 ), which suggests that GeoSteer-DM mainly targets memorization-associated geometry instead of just indiscriminately perturbing generative trajectories. Figure 4: GeoSteer-DM improves memorization–quality trade-offs across mitigation families. Mean SSCD to memorized training references versus CLIP prompt alignment (left) and FID (right) on memorized prompts. Connected markers show each method, including unmodified sampling, before and after adding GeoSteer-DM .

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We characterized memorization in diffusion models through the local spectral geometry of the generative field. Across training and generation, memorization manifests through a distinct spectral collapse–recovery dynamic: as models memorize during training, an intermediate-noise dominant mode emerges; during generation, entering a memorization basin corresponds to a transient spectral collapse around this leading direction. Local spectral geometry thus provides a unified framework for identifying when and how trajectories become committed to memorized outcomes. Acting on this geometric structure yields practical tools across the generative lifecycle: training-time spectral regularization, efficient detection, and inference-time trajectory steering, which scales to models as large as Stable Diffusion. While GeoSteer-DM employs a simple norm-preserving reflection along the leading singular mode, future work may leverage higher-order subspace projections or adaptive trajectory control. Overall, our findings demonstrate that local Jacobian geometry provides both a diagnostic and an actionable target for controlling memorization.

sections.heading: Detection baselines.
sections.text: We compare JER with the full temporal recovery diagnostic in Eq. ( 8 ) and three local geometric baselines. FLIPD Ross et al. (2025) estimates local intrinsic dimensionality from the score norm and a stochastic estimate of the score-Jacobian trace. The normal-bundle estimator Stanczuk et al. (2024) constructs a local geometric representation from independently perturbed score evaluations and estimates its dimension through an SVD; in our d = 1024 d=1024 controlled setting, we use the prescribed 4 ​ d = 4096 4d=4096 perturbed evaluations. Unless stated otherwise, all baselines are implemented and evaluated following the protocols and hyperparameter settings of their respective original works. We additionally evaluate unconditional score magnitude as a local sharpness baseline, motivated by Jeon et al. (2024) but distinct from their conditional memorization detector. Since the predictive orientation of this scalar statistic is not fixed a priori, its orientation and operating threshold are selected on the calibration set and then frozen for held-out evaluation. Detector runtime is measured independently of sampling and includes the model and derivative evaluations required to obtain each score. Temporal recovery requires nine full-Jacobian evaluations along the trajectory, whereas JER uses a single local query with two probe directions for DDIM and one for rectified flow. Full detection and runtime results are reported in Table 2 . Unlike FLIPD, which converts a trace estimate into LID using the noise scale and a score-norm term, JER normalizes by Jacobian energy and is invariant to J ↦ c ​ J J\mapsto cJ , separating the organization of curvature from its magnitude. We evaluate this distinction empirically in Sec. 5.1 , comparing both detection performance and computational cost.

sections.heading: E.1 GeoReg Training Baselines
sections.text: We compare GeoReg with several training-time baselines chosen to distinguish its spectral intervention from simpler mechanisms that can reduce memorization. Unless stated otherwise, all methods use the same model, training schedule, minibatches, and evaluation protocol as GeoReg.

sections.heading: Standard training.
sections.text: The unregularized baseline continues optimization using only ℒ base \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{base}} .

sections.heading: Tikhonov score regularization.
sections.text: Following the score regularization studied by Baptista et al. (2025) , we penalize the squared magnitude of the estimated score. In the noise-prediction parameterization this gives Φ Tik = ‖ ϵ θ ​ ( x t , t ) ‖ 2 2 d ​ b t 2 , \Phi_{\mathrm{Tik}}=\frac{\|\epsilon_{\theta}(x_{t},t)\|_{2}^{2}}{d\,b_{t}^{2}}, (36) where b t b_{t} denotes the diffusion noise scale. This baseline regularizes the magnitude of the learned score without explicitly constraining its local derivatives.

sections.heading: Reduced learning rate.
sections.text: As an optimization control, we halve the Adam learning rate after 10k training checkpoint. All methods share the same training history with learning rate 10 − 4 10^{-4} through 10k ; the reduced-LR baseline then continues ordinary diffusion training using only the base noise-prediction objective at 5 × 10 − 5 5\times 10^{-5} through 60k . This tests whether reduced memorization can be explained by slower continued optimization alone.

sections.heading: Ambient-style noisy training.
sections.text: We additionally consider a fixed-noisy-bank baseline inspired by Ambient Diffusion Daras et al. (2023) . At the training fork, each training example is corrupted once at diffusion index 50 50 , producing a fixed noisy training set used throughout the continuation. For timesteps up to this corruption level, training uses the ordinary noise-prediction objective; at larger timesteps, we use the corresponding noise-aware objective without restoring clean supervision. This changes the information supplied during training rather than directly regularizing the learned score or its Jacobian. Because the construction is adapted to our uniform-time noise-prediction setting, we refer to it as an Ambient-style baseline rather than a reproduction of the original method.

sections.heading: Regularization strengths.
sections.text: For the synthetic experiments, regularization coefficients are calibrated at the common training fork so that the initial auxiliary-loss parameter-gradient norm is approximately 10 % 10\% of the base-loss gradient norm. The reduced-learning-rate and Ambient-style controls do not use this calibration because they modify the optimization or training-data procedure rather than adding a regularization term.

sections.heading: E.2 Synthetic Data Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate GeoReg on three synthetic populations of increasing geometric complexity. In each setting, the training set is sampled once and then held fixed throughout optimization; only diffusion noise and timesteps are resampled during training. Evaluation uses independent samples from the known population distribution. The model is trained only on the fixed training coordinates and is not provided with component identities, latent coordinates, population parameters, or other information used to construct the datasets.

sections.heading: Gaussian80.
sections.text: The training set consists of N = 80 N=80 independent samples from a two-dimensional standard Gaussian, x ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I 2 ) . x\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{2}). No standardization is applied. This provides a full-dimensional unimodal setting in which attraction to individual training coordinates can be separated from multimodal or manifold structure.

The stratified training set allows us to examine copying together with mode coverage, component balance, and within-component variation.

sections.heading: Training and sampling.
sections.text: All synthetic experiments use a width- 128 128 noise-prediction MLP trained with Adam at learning rate 10 − 3 10^{-3} and batch size 512 512 for 30k updates, with methods sharing the same initial 5k -update unregularized prefix. The low dimensionality permits exact input-Jacobian computation. Geometric regularization is applied to at most 32 32 eligible states per minibatch at diffusion timesteps t ∈ { 5 , … , 100 } t\in\{5,\ldots,100\} , using the selection procedure specified for the corresponding experiment. Generation uses deterministic DDIM with 100 100 sampling steps. For each dataset and data seed, we fix 2,000 2{,}000 validation population samples, 10,000 10{,}000 final population samples, and a separate 10,000 10{,}000 -sample population-null set. The latter provides a population baseline for nearest-training-point statistics: population samples can naturally lie near the finite training set.

sections.heading: Evaluation.
sections.text: We distinguish copying from population-level distributional agreement. Copying is measured relative to the fixed finite training set. Sliced Wasserstein distance (SWD), distributional precision, and distributional recall are instead computed against independent samples from the underlying population. SWD measures agreement between the generated and population distributions through one-dimensional projections, while precision measures the fraction of generated samples lying within the estimated support of the population and recall measures the fraction of the population support covered by the generated distribution. These quantities are complementary. A model can produce individually plausible samples while covering only part of the population, resulting in high precision but lower recall. Conversely, increased coverage can be accompanied by additional mass outside the population support. SWD is sensitive to broader distributional discrepancies, including changes in relative mass across mixture components. None of these population metrics measures copying directly, which is why we report them together with nearest-training-point statistics.

sections.heading: E.4 Memorization and Generation-Quality Metrics
sections.text: For the controlled models, memorization is measured directly in the mean-centered grayscale pixel space used for training. Given a generated sample y y , let d 1 ​ ( y ) d_{1}(y) and d 2 ​ ( y ) d_{2}(y) denote its smallest and second-smallest Euclidean distances to the 4,096 training examples. We define the nearest-neighbor gap ratio r ⁡ ( y ) = d 1 ​ ( y ) d 2 ​ ( y ) + 10 − 10 , r(y)=\frac{d_{1}(y)}{d_{2}(y)+10^{-10}}, (37) and classify a generation as memorized when r ⁡ ( y ) < 1 3 . r(y)<\frac{1}{3}. (38) We report memorization rate together with the corresponding nearest-neighbor gap statistics. Generation quality is evaluated using FID with 2,048-dimensional Inception-v3 pool-3 features. For GeoReg, FID is computed from 50,000 generations against the full 4,096-image CelebA training set; for GeoSteer, it is computed from 500 generations per arm and checkpoint against a fixed 1,024-image CelebA reference set. We treat FID as a secondary metric in this controlled setting because direct reproduction of images in the finite reference set can itself improve FID.

sections.heading: GeoReg.
sections.text: We evaluate all training methods using the same ordinary deterministic DDIM sampling procedure. We report results through 60k updates, by which point the training objective has largely saturated, and do not continue these runs into the deliberately overtrained regime used separately to study memorization dynamics and GeoSteer. Training configurations and computational-cost measurements are given in Appendix D.4 .

sections.heading: Memorization detection.
sections.text: JER is evaluated at the 160k checkpoint for both generative dynamics in the main body. We report additional checkpoints in the appendix. Calibration uses 1,000 trajectories per sampler, obtained from ten sampling seeds with 100 generations each. A disjoint set of another 1,000 trajectories per sampler is reserved for evaluation. Threshold selection and baseline definitions are given in Appendix B.3 . Throughout our analyses, memorization rates are estimated from the generation cohorts used by each experiment; the differing evaluation sizes therefore produce small variations in the reported control rates across sections.

sections.heading: GeoSteer.
sections.text: We evaluate steering at 30 ​ k , 60 ​ k , 100 ​ k , 160 ​ k , 200 ​ k , 300 ​ k 30\mathrm{k},\,60\mathrm{k},\,100\mathrm{k},\,160\mathrm{k},\,200\mathrm{k},\,300\mathrm{k} updates. Each sampler–checkpoint pair contains 500 paired baseline and steered generations, obtained from five sampling seeds with 100 generations each. Within each pair, both trajectories begin from the same Gaussian initial state. For DDIM, steering resumes from sampler state 60 and is applied to transitions 60–98. For rectified flow, it resumes from state 20 and is applied to Euler updates 20–89. The geometric operator and sampler-specific formulation are given in Appendix C .

sections.heading: E.6 Stable Diffusion Evaluation
sections.text: We evaluate text-to-image mitigation using Stable Diffusion v1.4 at 512 × 512 512\times 512 resolution. Generation uses deterministic DDIM with 50 steps, η = 0 \eta=0 , and classifier-free guidance scale 7.5 7.5 .

sections.heading: Evaluation cohorts.
sections.text: The memorized cohort contains 500 prompts with known memorized reference images from the Wen et al. benchmark. We generate four paired deterministic samples per prompt, giving 2,000 generations per method. To evaluate behavior away from known memorization, we additionally use 100 prompts labeled as non-memorized in the corresponding ground-truth collection and generate one paired sample per prompt and method.

sections.heading: Metrics.
sections.text: Training-image similarity is measured using SSCD cosine similarity. For the memorized cohort, each generation is compared against the complete bank of 500 memorized references and assigned its maximum similarity; we additionally report the fraction satisfying SSCD ≥ 0.50 . \operatorname{SSCD}\geq 0.50. For the non-memorized control cohort, nearest-reference similarity is computed against the common Webster/LAION reference bank. Prompt fidelity is measured as the cosine similarity between normalized CLIP ViT-B/32 prompt and image embeddings. We additionally report FID using Inception-v3 pool-3 features against a fixed reference set of 10,000 LAION-derived images center-cropped and resized to 512 × 512 512\times 512 .

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We compare GeoSteer with the unmodified sampler and four inference-time mitigation methods: Ren et al. ( Ren et al., 2024 ) , RTA ( Somepalli et al., 2023b ) , Wen et al. ( Wen et al., 2024 ) , and Han et al. ( Han et al., 2026 ) . We additionally compose each method with GeoSteer to evaluate whether geometric steering provides complementary mitigation. All methods use the configurations reported for the corresponding experiments. To isolate the effect of the interventions, all methods are applied to every trajectory independently of detection, and each baseline–GeoSteer pair shares the same initial noise.

sections.heading: F.2 Singular-Value Dynamics of the Spectral Transition
sections.text: Section 3.2 summarizes the spectral transition using the relative spectral gap Δ 12 \Delta_{12} . Here, we further investigate the underlying singular-value dynamics and demonstrate how this transition manifests in stable rank.

sections.heading: The spectral collapse is driven by the leading singular value.
sections.text: At high noise, the spectrum remains nearly isotropic in both cohorts, with singular values near unity and stable rank approaching the ambient dimension. As denoising enters intermediate noise levels, all singular values increase, but σ 1 \sigma_{1} grows faster than the bulk spectrum (Figure 8 c–d). Because SR ⁡ ( J t ) = ∑ i σ i 2 / σ 1 2 \mathrm{SR}(J_{t})=\sum_{i}\sigma_{i}^{2}/\sigma_{1}^{2} , this relative overshoot of σ 1 \sigma_{1} induces the collapse in stable rank (Figure 8 a). Spectral recovery occurs when secondary singular values subsequently catch up to σ 1 \sigma_{1} .

sections.heading: Memorized trajectories exhibit earlier separation and stronger recovery.
sections.text: Along memorized trajectories, σ 1 \sigma_{1} decouples from σ 2 \sigma_{2} earlier in the sampling process and by a wider margin, causing stable rank to fall sooner. The two cohorts diverge most prominently at low noise: for memorized samples, the leading singular values reconverge toward a nearly common scale, consistent with the isotropic 1 / b t 1/b_{t} scaling expected near an isolated memorized state. Consequently, their stable rank recovers substantially. For non-memorized trajectories, σ 1 \sigma_{1} remains separated from the remaining spectrum, leaving the recovery incomplete. In absolute time, minimum stable rank is comparable across groups; the key distinguishing features are the earlier separation of σ 1 \sigma_{1} and its subsequent recovery, which Δ 12 \Delta_{12} captures more directly upon alignment at t ∗ t^{*} (Figure 1 a).

sections.heading: Local entropy rank.
sections.text: Local entropy rank ν ⁡ ( J t ) \nu(J_{t}) displays the same qualitative collapse–recovery profile across a narrower dynamic range (Figure 8 b). Because ν \nu integrates over the full singular spectrum, it is dominated by bulk modes rather than a single leading singular value. Nevertheless, memorized trajectories systematically recover toward a higher-rank spectrum at low noise, whereas non-memorized trajectories continue to decay. sections.heading: F.4 Spectral Effect of GeoReg-DM
sections.text: The main motivation for GeoReg-DM is the spectral organization that emerges as memorization develops during training. In this section, we investigate how our regularizer impacts this geometry. We evaluate GeoReg-DM and standard training across different fixed noised training states per timestep and checkpoint. sections.heading: GeoReg-DM reduces intermediate-noise spectral concentration.
sections.text: The clearest change appears in stable rank at intermediate noise levels. At t = 300 t=300 , GeoReg-DM systematically increases stable rank across all evaluated checkpoints, with mean paired differences ranging from + 34.6 +34.6 to + 95.8 +95.8 (Table 6 ). At t = 200 t=200 , this effect peaks at the 28k checkpoint ( + 122.2 +122.2 ) and remains positive through 60k steps. sections.heading: F.5 Validation of the JER Spectral Proxy
sections.text: JER replaces the nuclear norm in the Rényi-2 effective rank with an oriented trace, yielding a quantity that can be estimated efficiently from Jacobian contractions. This approximation is useful only if it preserves the spectral-dimensionality signal of the exact quantity. We therefore test this directly, independently of memorization labels and detector performance, on 128 frozen query states for which the full Jacobian spectrum can be computed. We compare the oriented trace-to-Frobenius proxy with the exact Rényi-2 effective rank defined in Appendix B.1 . As shown in Fig. 13 , the oriented trace-to-Frobenius proxy preserves the ordering of the exact Rényi-2 effective rank across query states, with Spearman correlations of 0.994 0.994 for DDIM and 0.978 0.978 for rectified flow. The proxy is conservative in magnitude, as expected from replacing the nuclear norm by the oriented trace, but the relationship remains strongly monotonic across both memorized and non-memorized states. Memorized states lie toward the high-rank end of the distribution and particularly close to the equality line. Thus, although JER is not intended as an unbiased numerical estimator of ER 2 \operatorname{ER}_{2} , it retains the spectral ordering relevant for discrimination while avoiding an explicit spectral decomposition. Exact Rényi-2 effective rank (horizontal axis) versus the deterministic oriented trace-to-Frobenius proxy (vertical axis) on frozen DDIM and rectified-flow query states. Colors distinguish memorized and non-memorized generations, and the dashed line denotes equality. The proxy is conservative in magnitude but closely preserves the ordering of the exact spectral quantity across states.

sections.text: We further evaluate JER on Stable Diffusion v1.4 using released collections of memorized and non-memorized prompts. Unlike the controlled experiments, the target in this benchmark is membership in these prompt collections rather than whether an individual generation reproduces a training example. This distinction is important because several diffusion memorization detectors exploit atypical conditional responses associated with memorized prompts.

sections.text: Under masked conditioning, conditional JER reaches 0.712 0.712 AUROC and 30.3 % 30.3\% TPR at 1 % 1\% FPR, compared with 0.671 0.671 for unconditional JER, and near-chance performance for the corresponding conditional score norm ( 0.513 0.513 ). Thus, the local spectral statistic remains informative at Stable Diffusion scale and captures structure beyond prediction magnitude alone. At the stringent operating point, its 30.3 % 30.3\% TPR is also close to the strongest detector in this setting, the Hessian score-difference statistic at 34.8 % 34.8\% .

sections.heading: What does the prompt benchmark measure?
sections.text: Performance changes markedly when the post-EOS conditioning tail is exposed. Conditional JER rises to 0.974 0.974 AUROC, while score-difference, Hessian, and anisotropy statistics reach 0.985 0.985 – 0.990 0.990 . This sensitivity is relevant to the interpretation of the benchmark. Many diffusion memorization detectors operate by identifying unusually strong or anisotropic conditional responses: such responses can characterize prompts associated with memorization, but do not by themselves establish that a particular generated image copies a training example. Indeed, the released prompt collections are themselves highly distinguishable from text alone: a character 3 3 – 5 5 -gram classifier reaches 0.986 0.986 AUROC and uppercase-character count reaches 0.968 0.968 . The conditioning comparison provides a concrete example of how this prompt structure can enter model-based scores. Masked and no-mask CLIP representations agree through the first EOS token, while the post-EOS tail remains available to U-Net cross-attention when it is not masked. Removing this tail at cross-attention reduces fixed-state epsilon-difference discrimination from 0.970 0.970 to 0.774 0.774 , close to its masked value of 0.783 0.783 . We therefore view the masked results as the more conservative evidence that JER transfers to a large pretrained diffusion model. The substantially higher no-mask results also expose a limitation of prompt-list evaluation: success can depend on prompt-source and conditioning structure whose relation to generation-level copying may not transfer to less curated prompt distributions.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2611.01775v1 [cs.LG] 01 Nov 2026 Spectral Signatures of Memorization Basins in Diffusion Trajectories Achref Jaziri * Goethe University FrankfurtFrankfurt am Main, Germany Martin MundtUniversity of BremenBremen, Germany Ahmed Imtiaz HumayunGoogleNew York, NY, USA Visvanathan RameshGoethe University FrankfurtFrankfurt am Main, Germany Abstract Diffusion models are known to reproduce individual examples from their training data as a form of memorization with implications for generalization, privacy, and downstream use. Recent work demonstrated that memorized training samples reside inside contiguous regions of the data/latent space known as basins of memorization – once a denoising trajectory enters a basin, under finite perturbations it irreversibly reproduces a memorized example. Prior empirical work on such basins in trained models has primarily focused on classifier-free guidance based detection and mitigation strategies in text-to-image models, leaving basin entry in trained diffusion trajectories and the formation of such basins largely uncharacterized. In this paper, we present a geometric characterization of memorization basins for conditional, unconditional, and rectified-flow-based diffusion models. We observe a characteristic signature in the local spectrum of the function geometry that distinguishes basin entry: the emergence of a dominant singular mode followed by a sharp spectral recovery. This signature appears at two timescales: along denoising trajectories during inference and over the course of training, with a markedly stronger presence along memorized trajectories. We further investigate whether these geometric signatures can be used to intervene on memorization. During training, we suppress memorization by acting on the dominant mode. At inference, we develop methods to identify trajectories entering memorization basins and steer them away. We find that these interventions remain effective even with low-dimensional approximations of the underlying geometry, and demonstrate that geometry-informed steering extends to large-scale text-to-image diffusion models. Together, our results corroborate that local spectral geometry provides a common basis for characterizing memorization and for suppressing, detecting, and steering away from it across training and generation. † † footnotetext: * Corresponding author: jaziri@em.uni-frankfurt.de. † \dagger shared last authorship. 1 Introduction Generative models are increasingly deployed as components of larger computational systems, where their outputs inform subsequent predictions, optimization, or decisions. Diffusion models exemplify this shift as they are deployed to generate molecular and protein structures ( Wu et al., 2024 ) , candidate solutions for combinatorial optimization ( Sun and Yang, 2023 ) , and actions and trajectories for planning and control ( Chi et al., 2025 ) . As diffusion models take on this broader role, it is important to understand how much information from their training data is retained in their generated samples. Diffusion models can closely reproduce individual training examples ( Carlini et al., 2023 ) , raising concerns around privacy, copyright, and generalization. However, memorization is not inherently undesirable. More broadly in deep learning, retaining information about individual or atypical training examples can contribute positively to generalization ( Feldman and Zhang, 2020 ) . In diffusion models, memorization is also highly selective. These models reproduce only a subset of their training examples, with susceptibility to memorization depending on properties of both the data and the learned distribution ( Carlini et al., 2023 ; Bonnaire et al., 2026 ) . More generally, these empirical observations regarding memorization and memory in deep learning have been connected to model geometry. Previous work has shown that retained training information can be reflected in local model geometry ( Nickl et al., 2023 ) and captured through compact spectral representations ( Jung et al., 2026 ) . In generative models, the manifold memorization hypothesis further associates memorized samples with locally constrained regions of the learned distribution ( Ross et al., 2025 ) . In this work, we posit that the constrained local geometry associated with memorization have a distinct temporal signature as trajectories evolve during denoising. We further investigate whether this geometry can be used to identify and intervene on memorized trajectories. More specifically, we ask: when does a denoising trajectory become committed to a memorized outcome, what spectral signature emerges, and can it guide intervention? We adopt the framework of memorization basins , defining them as regions from which a trajectory cannot escape a memorized outcome under bounded perturbations. Around basin entry, we empirically observe a distinct signature in the local Jacobian spectrum, accompanied by changes in perturbation sensitivity and generative dynamics. A related spectral pattern also emerges during training. At intermediate denoising steps, the input-output Jacobians develop a dominant singular mode, whereas low-noise spectra exhibit stronger rank recovery. We further investigate whether these geometric properties can be used to suppress memorization during training and to detect or redirect memorized trajectories during generation. To this end, we propose GeoReg-DM, which regularizes local Jacobian geometry to suppress memorization during training. For inference, we introduce Jacobian Effective Rank (JER), which uses the endpoint of the spectral signature to detect memorized generations, and GeoSteer-DM, which exploits dominant singular directions to redirect memorized trajectories. Across diffusion and rectified-flow models, our results establish local spectral geometry as a unifying perspective on how memorization emerges and can be controlled across training and generation. 2 Related Work Memorization and geometry in generative models. Memorization is a longstanding phenomenon in overparameterized neural networks, which can retain individual or atypical training examples while still generalizing ( Feldman and Zhang, 2020 ) . In generative models, memorization becomes directly observable through training-example reproduction ( Carlini et al., 2023 ; Somepalli et al., 2023a ) , with subsequent work studying how it develops during diffusion training and how retained examples are represented within the model ( Bonnaire et al., 2026 ; Hintersdorf et al., 2024 ; Kowalczuk et al., 2025 ) . Local geometry provides a complementary perspective on generative distributions ( Meng et al., 2021 ) , including intrinsic dimensionality, manifold structure, and spectral regimes across diffusion time ( Stanczuk et al., 2024 ; Humayun et al., 2025 ; Ventura et al., 2025 ) . Memorization has specifically been associated with locally constrained or sharp regions of the learned distribution ( Ross et al., 2025 ; Jeon et al., 2024 ) , while related analyses study denoiser-Jacobian eigenstructure ( Kadkhodaie et al., 2024 ) , variance-dependent loss of tangent dimensions ( Achilli et al., 2024 ) , and log-probability anisotropy ( Asthana and Belagiannis, 2026 ) . We build on these analyses by resolving spectral geometry along individual trajectories and across training, and by using its singular directions for intervention. Memorization mitigation and geometric control. Existing mitigation methods intervene during training through the data or optimization procedure ( Dutt et al., 2025 ; Shah et al., 2025 ) , or during generation through conditioning, attention, model predictions, initial noise, and internal model components ( Somepalli et al., 2023a ; Ren et al., 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ; Wen et al., 2024 ; Han et al., 2026 ) . Separately, geometric editing methods use Jacobian singular directions and learned subspaces to control generation ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Gaintseva et al., 2026b ; Gaintseva et al., 2026a ) . Our approach connects these perspectives by using memorization-associated local spectral geometry as an intervention target during training and as a signal for detection and control during generation. 3 THE DYNAMICS AND GEOMETRY OF MEMORIZATION 3.1 Memorization Basins The manifold memorization hypothesis ( Ross et al., 2025 ) associates memorization with locally constrained regions of the learned distribution that restrict the effective degrees of freedom of generated samples. We now test whether these properties scale to Stable Diffusion v1.4, where text conditioning and high dimensionality make full Jacobian construction infeasible. Using matrix-free estimates of the guidance-residual Jacobian (Appendix C.2 ), we evaluate GeoSteer-DM across 500 prompts with known memorized references (2,000 generations per setup). Geometric steering scales to text-to-image diffusion. Using matrix-free estimates of local guidance geometry, GeoSteer-DM substantially reduces training-reference similarity and the fraction of generations exceeding the SSCD copying threshold, while generation quality and a modest reduction in prompt alignment (Figure 4 ; full metrics in Appendix F.12 ). This demonstrates that local geometric steering scales to large-scale text-conditioned models. Representative samples in Figure 15 illustrate this and show that steering suppresses memorization while preserving core prompt semantics. GeoSteer-DM complements existing mitigation strategies. Unlike existing methods that intervene via text conditioning, attention, model predictions, or initial noise, GeoSteer-DM acts directly on local Jacobian geometry. As shown in Figure 4 , adding GeoSteer-DM consistently shifts each baseline toward lower reference similarity with minimal impact on CLIP score or FID. Furthermore, these shifts are smaller on non-memorized control prompts (Appendix F.12 ), which suggests that GeoSteer-DM mainly targets memorization-associated geometry instead of just indiscriminately perturbing generative trajectories. Across training and generation, memorization manifests through a distinct spectral collapse–recovery dynamic: as models memorize during training, an intermediate-noise dominant mode emerges; during generation, entering a memorization basin corresponds to a transient spectral collapse around this leading direction. Local spectral geometry thus provides a unified framework for identifying when and how trajectories become committed to memorized outcomes. Acting on this geometric structure yields practical tools across the generative lifecycle: training-time spectral regularization, efficient detection, and inference-time trajectory steering, which scales to models as large as Stable Diffusion. While GeoSteer-DM employs a simple norm-preserving reflection along the leading singular mode, future work may leverage higher-order subspace projections or adaptive trajectory control. Overall, our findings demonstrate that local Jacobian geometry provides both a diagnostic and an actionable target for controlling memorization.
